# Outline - An Unforgettable Event (Article)

Task: An international magazine has invited readers to send in an article called "An Unforgettable Event". Describe an event in your life that you will never forget, explain why it was so memorable, and say what effect remembering important events can have on people.

Planned structure: open with a vivid account of the moment the event began, using direct speech to bring it to life. Then describe what happened next and what made it special. Add a personal reflection on which part of the experience stays with you most. Finish with a general paragraph on why recalling memorable events is good for us.

The article should engage a wide magazine readership, so the tone can be personal and lively while staying well organised.

# Research Notes - School Exchange Programmes

Short-term school exchanges usually last between a few weeks and a full school year. Students attend classes at a partner school abroad and live with a host family, which gives them daily contact with the local language and culture.

Common benefits reported by exchange students are greater independence, improved language skills, new friendships and a better understanding of other ways of life. Many students describe the host family as the most important part of the experience.

Some programmes are fully funded by schools, governments or foundations, while others are paid for by the families. Selection is often based on school results, behaviour and recommendations from teachers.

Psychologists use the term "nostalgia" for warm memories of the past. Research on nostalgia suggests that recalling meaningful events can improve mood and give people a sense of connection and meaning.

# Outline - Local Quill Report

The report presents Local Quill, a writing feedback system that runs entirely on the user's own machine. Section 1 introduces the privacy problem with cloud-hosted LLMs, the two target writing categories (academic essays and fictional prose) and the research question: can 8B-parameter local LLMs supported by RAG reach results comparable to GPT-5-nano, measured with G-Eval?

Section 2 covers the state of the art: the transformer architecture and the rise of LLMs, model compression through quantization, Ollama as a local runtime for quantized GGUF models, and retrieval-augmented generation. Section 3 describes the data: 12 publicly available PDF documents with essay writing guides, fiction writing guides and test materials such as Cambridge English sample responses.

# Assessment Criteria - Tertiary Project Report

## Problem and research question
The report states a clear problem, explains why it matters and formulates a research question that can be answered with the chosen method.

## Background and sources
The state of the art is explained accurately and supported by cited sources. Direct quotations are marked and referenced.

## Method and results
The methods are described in enough detail to be repeated. Results are presented clearly and linked back to the research question.

## Structure and language
The report follows a logical structure with numbered sections and gives an overview of the structure in the introduction. The language is formal, precise and objective, and technical terms are explained when first used.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was described by Lewis et al. in 2020. A retriever finds relevant passages in an external document store, and these passages are added to the prompt so that the generator can base its answer on them.

G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023) uses a strong LLM as a judge. The judge receives evaluation criteria, generates evaluation steps through chain-of-thought, and then scores the output.

# Research Notes - Local LLMs and RAG

The transformer architecture was introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need" by Vaswani et al. It replaced recurrence with self-attention, which lets the model relate every token to every other token in the input.

Quantization stores model weights with fewer bits, for example 4-bit or 8-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats. This reduces memory use and speeds up inference on consumer hardware, usually with a small loss in quality. Post-training quantization converts an already trained model, while quantization-aware training simulates the lower precision during training.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was described by Lewis et al. in 2020. A retriever finds relevant passages in an external document store, and these passages are added to the prompt so that the generator can base its answer on them.

# Research Notes - The Hobbit

The Hobbit, or There and Back Again, by J. R. R. Tolkien was first published in 1937. It was written for children and is set in the same world as The Lord of the Rings, which was published later, in 1954-1955.

The main character, Bilbo Baggins, is a hobbit: a small, home-loving person who lives in a comfortable hole at Bag End in the Shire. The wizard Gandalf chooses him to join Thorin Oakenshield and twelve other dwarves as their burglar.

The dwarves want to win back their home and treasure in the Lonely Mountain (Erebor), which the dragon Smaug took from them long ago. On the journey Bilbo meets trolls, goblins, Gollum, giant spiders and wood-elves. Smaug is killed by Bard the Bowman at Lake-town, and the story ends with the Battle of Five Armies.

Common themes of the book are courage, growing up, the value of home and the dangers of greed.

## Sherlock Holmes
Consulting detective living at 221B Baker Street. Known for sharp observation, cold reasoning and a talent for disguise. He takes the King's case for the challenge as much as for the fee. ## Dr. John Watson
Holmes's friend and former flatmate, and the narrator of the story. He has recently married and moved out of Baker Street, but visits Holmes again during this case. He admires Holmes's methods and helps him by throwing the smoke rocket at Briony Lodge.

Born in New Jersey, a former contralto at La Scala and prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw. She lives at Briony Lodge in St. John's Wood. Clever and quick, she sees through Holmes's disguise and leaves England before he can take the photograph.

## Irene Adler
Born in New Jersey, a former contralto at La Scala and prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw. She lives at Briony Lodge in St. John's Wood. Clever and quick, she sees through Holmes's disguise and leaves England before he can take the photograph.

## Godfrey Norton
A handsome, dark lawyer of the Inner Temple who visits Irene Adler often. He marries her in a hurried ceremony at the Church of St. Monica.

Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, hereditary King of Bohemia. He first visits Holmes masked, calling himself Count Von Kramm. He is about to marry Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen and fears the scandal Adler's photograph could cause.

The landlady at Baker Street. In this story she is called Mrs. Turner, although in most other Holmes stories the landlady is Mrs. Hudson.

The story takes place in London in March 1888. Holmes's rooms at 221B Baker Street are the base of the investigation: a sitting room with a fire where clients are received, and a bedroom where Holmes keeps his disguises.

Other places in the story are the Inner Temple, where Godfrey Norton has his chambers, and the Church of St. Monica in the Edgeware Road, where the wedding takes place.

# Character Notes - The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

## Dorothy
A young girl from a farm in Kansas who lives with her Aunt Em and Uncle Henry. Kind, practical and determined to get home. She wears the silver shoes of the Wicked Witch of the East and carries a basket for food on the journey.

## Toto
Dorothy's small black dog, who keeps her cheerful. He travels everywhere in her arms or at her feet.

## The Scarecrow
Made of straw and found on a pole in a cornfield. He believes he has no brains and wants the Wizard to give him some, yet he often comes up with the group's best plans. He cannot be hurt by falling and does not get tired or hungry, but he fears fire.

A woodman made entirely of tin, who wants a heart. He is very tender-hearted and careful not to hurt any living creature. If he cries, his jaws rust, so he needs his oil-can. His sharp axe is often useful on the journey.

# Dracula - Outline

Bram Stoker's epistolary novel (1897) is told through diaries, letters and newspaper clippings. The young solicitor Jonathan Harker travels to Transylvania to help Count Dracula buy an estate in England. He soon realises that he is a prisoner in the castle and that the Count is a vampire. Dracula sails to England on the ship Demeter and lands at Whitby, where he begins to prey on Lucy Westenra, the close friend of Jonathan's fiancée, Mina Murray.

Dr. John Seward, one of Lucy's suitors, calls in his old teacher, Professor Abraham Van Helsing. Despite blood transfusions from Lucy's fiancé Arthur Holmwood (later Lord Godalming), Seward, Quincey Morris and Van Helsing, Lucy dies and becomes a vampire. The men destroy her in her tomb, and Arthur drives the stake through her heart. Jonathan, who has escaped and married Mina, joins them, and the group starts to destroy the boxes of earth that Dracula needs to rest in London.

## Dr. John Seward
Director of a lunatic asylum near Carfax and a former suitor of Lucy. He keeps his diary on a phonograph. He narrates many chapters.

## Professor Abraham Van Helsing
A Dutch doctor, philosopher and Seward's old teacher. He knows the most about vampires and leads the group. He gave Lucy peace after her death and now guides the hunt for Dracula.

## Arthur Holmwood, Lord Godalming
Lucy's fiancé, who inherited his father's title. He drove the stake through Lucy's heart. His money and position help the group.

## Quincey Morris
A brave, plain-speaking American from Texas and another former suitor of Lucy. He carries a large Bowie knife and is loyal to his friends.

## Count Dracula
An ancient Transylvanian noble and vampire who has come to England. He can command animals, change form and influence those whose blood he has taken.

William Shakespeare's tragedy (around 1600) is set at the royal court of Denmark. Romeo, a young Montague, sneaks into a Capulet feast and falls in love with Juliet, the Capulets' daughter. They meet again that night at her balcony and agree to marry, and Friar Lawrence marries them in secret the next day, hoping the match will end the feud.

Soon afterwards Juliet's cousin Tybalt kills Romeo's friend Mercutio in a street fight, and Romeo kills Tybalt in revenge. The Prince banishes Romeo to Mantua. Juliet's parents, unaware of her marriage, arrange for her to marry Count Paris. Friar Lawrence gives Juliet a potion that will make her appear dead for a time, so she can escape the wedding, and he sends a letter to tell Romeo of the plan. The letter never reaches him.

# Setting - The Capulet Tomb

The scene takes place at night in a churchyard in Verona, where the Capulet family monument stands. The monument is a stone vault where the family's dead are laid. Juliet was placed there after her apparent death, and her cousin Tybalt, recently killed, also lies inside.

The churchyard is dark and quiet. The ground is loose from the digging of graves, and yew trees grow there. The visitors carry torches, which can be seen from far away.
